insights: Authentication checks canonical entry identities, snapshot membership, exact complete reachable closure and topological order. It grants no theorem authority; domain-specific admission still replays proofs.

Borrowed bundle encoding avoids a second JSON tree while preserving canonical key order and integer/depth constraints. Existing adversarial tests compare its bytes/hash/rejections with generic canonical encoding.

First-order admission uses a context subset of explicit dependencies before declaring/importing an entry. General reuse must preserve these direct import boundaries and sealed transitive dependencies.

A future reused first-order context must pair sealed proof entries with authenticated registry identities. An arbitrary logic::Context may contain caller-chosen IDs and cannot serve as a generic content-hash verdict cache.

CheckedBundle::merge requires the same snapshot and checks bounded union size. ProofContext pure reuse instead authenticates every complete incoming view and exposes only its laws; these are deliberately different policies.

The common verifier keeps proof domains separate, authenticates searchable interfaces against typed payloads, and rejects unsupported domains. Database generalisations must be translated to an admitted proof domain, not accepted from a new semantics string.
Per-entry, complete-view, dependency-count/depth and catalogue limits are distinct. Increasing one domain transport allowance cannot imply larger proof-kernel work budgets.

Membership path/leaf hashing repeats across entries sharing witnesses. Potential bounded structural deduplication needs profiling and exact-byte keys; it could save authentication work but must never skip membership or proof checking.

Canonicalization currently serializes full bytes before length checking; streaming bounded hashing could lower transient memory, requiring byte-identical key ordering, numeric/depth rejection and frontend transport-limit tests before replacement.
status: Full source review and existing tests; follow-up optimisations unimplemented and unmeasured.
